sources.title: Michael A. McDonnell: Masters of Empire, publisher introduction
sources.note: Author research-book description: Odawa at Mackinac, kinship, commerce and influence on colonial powers. Separate full excerpt failed to load; no claim depends on unseen excerpt.

sources.title: Mackinac State Historic Parks: Canoes
sources.note: Regional fur-trade transport context. Does not claim Odawa alone invented all canoe forms, or attribute every French cargo vessel to Odawa makers.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian: Odawa moccasins, 20/2175
sources.note: Direct museum object label: circa 1825 to 1835, Indiana, purchased at Crown Point; hide, cloth, silk, beads, cuff/vamp decoration. No exact manufacture year assigned.

sources.title: Cheyenne Kiogima: Making an aankinaagan, LTBB Tribal Newsletter, February 2019
sources.note: First-person account on printed pp. 1 and 14 (PDF indices 0 and 13). Birchbark and jack pine roots, Renee Wasson Dillard teacher, grandfather-harvested bark about 20 years old. Descriptive history, not infant-care advice.

sources.title: Detroit Historical Society: Chief Pontiac
sources.note: Selected 1763 failed surprise attack and siege, loosely organized alliance. Does not universalize Pontiac as sovereign of all Odawa or repeat uncertain birthplace and sensational personal judgements.

sources.title: Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma: Notable Moments in Tribal History
sources.note: Tribal archives and historian David Dry contributions. Greenville, otter signatures, Ohio removals, termination/restoration. Treaty negotiation date July 28 not confused with August 3 treaty signature date.

sources.title: Adawe Cultural Center: Treaty of Seneca, 1867
sources.note: Official tribal explanation of Kansas land fraud, Shawnee purchase and removal. Approximate acreage and costs not needed in prose.

sources.title: Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma: Notable People in Tribal History
sources.note: Lizzie Lavore Wolfe reading/teaching and 1916 letter; family reminiscence of Clarence King and dog Biscuit. Anecdote explicitly attributed, not generalized. Extraordinary claimed ages for Jane King and first-patent superlatives not adopted.

sources.title: Laurentian University Indigenous Student Affairs: Language Learning
sources.note: Intro explicitly identifies Odawa dialect; Beginner Phrases table Aanii! Aaniish naa? / Hi! How are you?/How are things? Direct text inspected.

sources.title: Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians: Official tribal introduction
sources.note: September 21, 1994 federal reaffirmation and Michigan community context. No current membership/employment totals adopted.

sources.title: Little River Band of Ottawa Indians: Official introduction
sources.note: Direct homepage identifies descent from Grand River Ottawa Bands, Manistee/Pere Marquette/Grand River history, and 1994 reaffirmation. Separate modern government from LTBB.

sources.title: Adawe Cultural Center: Ottawa History
sources.note: Official Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma self-identification, Great Lakes/Ohio roots and nineteenth-century Kansas/Oklahoma homelands. Supports later-phase mapping recommendation only.

sources.title: Adawe Cultural Center: Language
sources.note: Current community language classes and teaching resources, including Little Traverse materials. No claim to an unchanged single spelling across all communities.

sources.title: Ho-Chunk Nation: About
sources.note: Official homeland and present governmental branches. Oral tradition identified as such; speculative three-ice-age chronology not adopted.

sources.title: Milwaukee Public Museum: Ho-Chunk History
sources.note: Direct text; European encounters, forced removals, Wisconsin persistence and seasonal work. No population estimates, archaeological lineage certainty or Nicolet exact landing site adopted.

sources.title: Milwaukee Public Museum: Ho-Chunk Culture
sources.note: Original indexed text supports storage and river transport; direct new-domain fetch fails. Distinct from history document, selected nonoverlapping material. Speculative matrilineal reconstruction and healing efficacy not used.

sources.title: Milwaukee Public Museum: Kinship
sources.note: Original indexed institutional text: Ho-Chunk clan names and responsibilities. Direct fetch failed; query "clan relatives provided names" "Ho-Chunk" reproduces selected passage. Does not assert unchanged prehistoric kinship system.

sources.title: Museum of Wisconsin Art: Weaving a Legacy, Ho-Chunk Black Ash Basketry
sources.note: Exhibition publication, 16 pages. Object Aesthetics: family preparation, carving, weaving and transmission. Economic context: roadside sales and inventories.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian: Alvina Foss basket, NMAI_408010
sources.note: Object record: Ho-Chunk Wisconsin artist Alvina Foss, dated 1990 to 2000; black ash/brown ash splints, wood and synthetic dyes. Date remains a range, no invented midpoint.

sources.title: HoChunk Renaissance: Three Sisters Garden
sources.note: Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska program report, September 9, 2021; fourth sunflower, students and volunteers, harvest sharing. Does not claim all historic Ho-Chunk gardens followed this exact model.

sources.title: Ho-Chunk Nation Department of Agriculture: FY2025 report
sources.note: Page 1 reports CSA pilot with 29 participants and radishes in Tribal Elder Food Box Program. Completed achievements separated from future goals.

sources.title: Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska, HoChunk Renaissance: Program History
sources.note: Only program-history section used: founding 2001, teaching teams and 2003 classes. The lower tribal-history compilation contains contradictory dates and garbled text and is not used.

sources.title: Ho-Chunk Nation: Official homepage greeting
sources.note: Indexed original heading: Hocąk Wazijacira Hižąkiišąną Hįįnį Karagiwiną / The Ho-Chunk Nation greets each and every one of you. Direct fetch repeatedly times out; exact indexed institutional text verified. No screenshot claim.

sources.title: Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska: Official government website
sources.note: Official sovereign-nation mission and self-identification as Ho-chunks (Winnebago). Separate modern government, not a Wisconsin district.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Accepted shared narrative for Odawa and Ottawa Oklahoma after reviewing official tribal identity and 1867 relocation accounts. Distinct modern governments and the anachronistic imported Oklahoma date remain explicit in public prose.
batchIdentityNotes.mapEvidence: odawa index 1492 to 1500, decoded world-1492 multipolygon bbox [-87.7707,42.4912,-80.3078,46.2640]. ottawa-oklahoma index 1492 to 1500, bbox [-94.8951,36.8203,-94.7187,36.8797], a tiny northeastern Oklahoma later homeland. Original dates preserved; opening explicitly flags Oklahoma anachronism.

proposedExistingAssociation.justification: Official tribal history links Oklahoma community to Great Lakes/Ohio roots through Kansas removal and 1867 purchase. Draft devotes explicit passages to Ohio removal, Kansas/Oklahoma relocation, termination/restoration, Oklahoma language/family continuity, and distinct modern governments.

batchIdentityNotes.limitations: No merger with Ojibwe or Potawatomi records. Introductory outline does not establish 1492 political boundaries. Pontiac is described as coalition leader, not king of all Odawa. Modern language sample explicitly Odawa dialect; no precontact readable manuscript claimed.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Single Ho-Chunk people narrative; distinguishes Wisconsin and Nebraska modern governments. No broader Siouan-language peoples absorbed.
batchIdentityNotes.mapEvidence: Index 1492 to 1500; world-1492 polygon bbox [-91.9611,41.4543,-87.3963,44.6949], Wisconsin/northern Illinois and adjoining upper Midwest. Public opening treats this as broad map coverage.
batchIdentityNotes.limitations: Does not assert that all nearby effigy mounds or all ancient canoe finds have a proven Ho-Chunk identity. Modern Nebraska gardening is explicitly regional and dated. Museum clan account is historical description, not an invented unchanged prehistoric constitution.
